h: A township that lived on into the 1960s
p: What makes Auchindrain so moving is how recently it was a working community. Families shared the land here for generations under an old Highland system where tenants worked the fields together, and the township kept going long after most others had been cleared or abandoned. The last tenant didn't leave until the 1960s, which means some of the houses show the change from very old ways of living to more modern comforts, sometimes side by side.

Take your time and read the stories that go with the buildings. Some of the houses are furnished to show particular periods, so you can compare a dark, simple longhouse with a cottage that has a proper range and a few home comforts. The barns and byres tell you a lot about how central animals were to daily life. It's a quiet, reflective sort of place rather than a high-energy family attraction, but children who enjoy exploring tend to find it fascinating.
Allow a couple of hours. A visitor centre at the entrance is the place to get oriented and pick up the background before you head down the track.

The A83 between Inveraray and Lochgilphead is a lovely drive, and you can combine it with other stops nearby. Crarae Garden, cared for by the National Trust for Scotland, is just a little further south on the shore of Loch Fyne, with a woodland gorge and rhododendrons that are glorious in late spring. Back in Inveraray, the castle, home of the Dukes of Argyll, and the old jail make great companions, and the head of the loch is famous for its seafood if you fancy a taste of Loch Fyne before heading home.
